- `TODOER_AUTH_ADMIN_EMAILS` grants deployment administrator access to matching

- Administrators use **Settings → Account security → Deployment authentication**.

- Disabling Google hides its button and denies its start/callback endpoints.

Passwords use Argon2id with independent salts and accept 15–128 characters.
Email signup sends a single-use verification link expiring after one hour; the
account and its initial workspace are created transactionally after verification.
Pending passwords are stored only as hashes. Google accounts can add a password
from Account security after a recent Google sign-in; this retains the same user
and task data. Accounts are never silently joined by matching email addresses.

Forgot-password responses are generic and reset tokens are hashed, single-use,
valid for 30 minutes and tied to the account security epoch and current verified
email. Email links carry tokens in fragments, which the browser removes from
history before submitting them in a JSON request. Password resets retain MFA and
require an enrolled authenticator/recovery code or a verified passkey when MFA is
active. Password changes/resets revoke all sessions and invalidate outstanding
security proofs. Session issuance checks the epoch in the same write transaction
as issuing the new session. Recent-session checks are repeated after queued work.

## MFA and WebAuthn

Account security can enroll a TOTP authenticator, add/remove named passkeys, and
rotate recovery codes. Sensitive changes require a full sign-in within five
minutes. Enrollment revokes other sessions and displays ten single-use recovery
codes once; store them before signing in again. TOTP seeds are encrypted with
ChaCha20-Poly1305 under a domain-separated deployment key and owner-bound associated
data. Accepted time steps cannot be reused. Recovery codes are stored as hashes.
Back up the stable server key: changing it prevents decrypting existing TOTP seeds.

WebAuthn uses webauthn-rs, validates the configured public origin/RP ID and requires
user verification for passkeys. Challenge state is bounded, single-use, expires
after five minutes, and stays on the server, bound to the initiating browser or
session and the account security epoch. Credential IDs are globally unique; stored
counters and backup flags are updated after verification. Password and Google
sign-in require a second factor when any MFA method is enrolled; a user-verified
passkey can sign in directly. Credentials remain tied to their RP hostname, so
localhost test credentials will not work for the production hostname.

The current challenge store is process-local. A restart interrupts incomplete
ceremonies; retrying starts a fresh challenge. Persisted accounts, credentials,
policy and sessions survive restart. SQLite deployments should run one app process
for these flows (or require sticky routing before introducing multiple workers).

## Sign-in return paths and security freshness

Unauthenticated HTML page navigation redirects to `/signin?next=…`, preserving
its local path and query. APIs retain JSON 401 responses. Security mutations
require authentication within five minutes; an expired proof returns the
`reauthentication_required` error and opens a sign-in confirmation dialog.
Signing in returns to the selected security section so the user can retry the
action. Passwords and other sensitive form values are not persisted for replay.
New email-based passkey sign-ins use their own validated return path rather than
inheriting a prior MFA attempt. Failed MFA codes keep the five-minute pending flow
available for a throttled retry; successful verification consumes it once.
Displayed recovery codes can be downloaded locally as a plain text file.

Password changes use a dedicated modal with matching new-password fields.
Accounts with an existing password must also provide their current password;
Google/passkey-only accounts can set their first password after a fresh sign-in.
The server checks confirmation, verifies the current password using the bounded
password-worker pool, and rechecks credentials before committing the change.
Save failures release the modal controls; closing clears the password fields.

# Bounded agent plans and destinations

Bulk operations use the application's existing mutation methods. A write outside a bulk transaction uses an immediate SQLite transaction; a write inside one uses a savepoint. An outer guard rolls back every uncommitted bulk change, including history, reference indexing and other database side effects. There is no second implementation of task mutation rules.

`POST /api/v1/bulk/preview` accepts an `operations` array. Each operation has `op`, a task ID or full stable task reference, its expected `revision`, and the operation's fields:

| `op` | Fields beyond ID and revision |
| --- | --- |
| `update` | Optional `title`, `description`; at least one is required |
| `move` | `destination` list ID; explicit `acknowledge_access_change` when required |
| `trash`, `restore` | No additional fields |
| `tags` | `tags`, containing existing names or `{ "id": "TAG_UUID" }` selectors |
| `section` | Nullable `section_id` |
| `reparent` | Nullable `parent_id`; same-list rules apply |

Tag names are resolved to existing IDs in their home before preview. A missing tag returns an actionable error; create it with the individual task-tag operation first. Bulk preview never creates tag identities.

Unknown fields are rejected. There are no create operations and no bulk completion operation in this contract. Completion can create recurring occurrences, so its generated resources are not represented by this create-free preview. Use the ordinary task update endpoint for completion.

Preview executes the real operations and rolls them back. It returns an actor-bound `preview_id`, `expected_hash`, `expires_at`, and ordered `steps` with canonical operations and before/after states. Task states include IDs, titles, revisions, placement, completion/deletion flags, tag names, a description excerpt of at most 120 characters, and a full-description hash. Move steps include their audience-change preview. Description hashes detect edits without returning whole descriptions in every step.

Plans expire after ten minutes. A request supports 1–50 operations and at most 500 affected task states across its steps; a stored plan is capped at 1 MiB. At most 100 unexpired plans are retained per actor. Subtree operations review descendants as well as the root; reparenting also reviews new ancestors that the shared rules may reopen.

`POST /api/v1/bulk/apply` accepts only `preview_id`, `expected_hash`, and `idempotency_key`. It executes the server-stored operations. Every step checks the reviewed task states, list revisions, effective permission audience and move preview against current data, then runs the common mutation method with live authorization. A changed descendant or audience invalidates the plan even when the root revision is unchanged. A later failure rolls back earlier successful steps.

A successful apply records its complete result in the same transaction. Retrying the same actor/key and identical preview/hash returns that result without repeating writes. Reusing a key with a different preview or hash conflicts. A retry rechecks current access to the result's historical lists and the tasks' current lists before returning any stored content. A different actor or credential cannot reuse another actor's plan. An expired or stale plan requires a new preview.

Destination endpoints return small authorized results rather than the account's complete contents:

| Method and path | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/v1/destinations/search?prefix=TEXT&limit=20` | Up to 30 accessible, active list IDs and titles; literal SQL wildcard characters are escaped |
| `GET /api/v1/destinations/resolve?destination=ID_OR_EXACT_TITLE` | Prefer an accessible exact ID, then exact title matches; duplicate titles return `ambiguous` and choices |
| `GET /api/v1/destinations/resolve?default_key=capture&fallback_inbox=true` | Use the saved default; optionally try the saved `inbox` default, then an accessible exact `Inbox` title |
| `GET /api/v1/destinations/preferences` | Only this user's preferences whose destinations are still accessible |
| `POST /api/v1/destinations/preferences` | Save `{ "key": "capture", "list_id": "LIST_ID" }`; requires current write access to that destination |

Resolution returns `status` (`resolved`, `ambiguous`, or `missing`), optional `destination`, bounded `choices`, and `has_more`. Exact-title comparisons preserve case and Unicode spelling. Explicit input never silently falls back to another destination when it is missing or ambiguous. No conversation state or model guess chooses a destination.

Preferences belong to the authenticated user, and scoped credentials can access only defaults pointing to lists currently within their grant. Keys contain 1–40 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, underscores or hyphens; each user has at most 100. Saving a preference updates that key; it does not create or rename a list. Browser bootstrap can save the actual inbox ID instead of relying on a title heuristic.

Domain tests cover nested savepoint rollback, preview rollback, atomic apply failures, stale descendants, hash/key binding, actor binding, expiry, permission loss, exact retries and bounded authorized destination resolution. Run `cargo test --locked agent_ops::tests --lib`.

# CLI browser login

The standalone Rust CLI uses REST; it does not open the application database.

    todoer --url https://todoer.example login --permission write
    todoer auth-status
    todoer --json list
    todoer logout

TODOER_URL selects the server. TODOER_TOKEN overrides a saved login.
Use --no-browser to open the printed authorization URL yourself. Login waits
300 seconds by default; --timeout accepts 10–600 seconds.

The CLI requests write access by default; pass `--permission read` or
`--permission admin` to change the maximum offered at approval. The browser
approval chooses read, write or admin access within that maximum and specific spaces
and/or lists. Space access includes future lists. Individual list access does
not expose its entire space. Current membership and permissions always clamp
the credential's access. Scoped credentials cannot administer account settings.
All resources requires explicit approval.

Login uses a loopback callback, state and S256 PKCE. Requests expire after ten
minutes; approval codes expire after two minutes and are single use. Tokens expire after 30 days by default. You can instead choose “Never expires”
at approval and revoke access later in Settings → Connected tools. The
“Never expires” option requires a CLI version that supports permanent logins.
Run login
again to renew an expired token. HTTPS is required except for
local development. This handshake is separate from MCP OAuth; CLI credentials
have the REST audience and cannot authenticate to MCP.

Credentials are stored per server in credentials.json under TODOER_CONFIG_DIR,
otherwise XDG_CONFIG_HOME/todoer, otherwise ~/.config/todoer. Unix permissions
are 0700 for the directory and 0600 for the file; writes are atomic. The server
stores only a token hash. Command output never prints the issued token.

Logout revokes the saved credential before removing it locally. On a server
failure it retains the local credential so revocation can be retried. It does
not unset an environment token. Credentials can also be revoked under Settings
→ Connected tools. Auth-status reports local metadata, not a live validity check.

Endpoints: POST /api/cli/login/start, browser GET/POST /cli/authorize,
POST /api/cli/login/token and POST /api/cli/login/revoke.

# Account job status

`/settings/jobs` is a read-only browser page; `/api/v1/jobs` exposes the same
bounded metadata to a browser session or an account-wide admin REST credential.
Read/write credentials and any list- or workspace-bounded credential are rejected,
even when the bounded credential includes admin. Authentication and the common
live credential lookup run for each request. Revoked/expired credentials and
revoked browser sessions cannot read the page or API.

The view includes only reminder jobs whose recipient is the current account,
email/push digest jobs owned by that account, and invitation delivery jobs whose
inviter is that account. It does not enumerate other accounts or grant a workspace
owner access to other members' notification queues. No task title/description,
recipient address, invitation token, transport endpoint, device key, lease token,
lease owner or raw provider error is selected for the response.

Rows show queue/job ID, kind, channel, status, attempts, available time and lease
expiry. Push rows additionally show pending/sent/dead device delivery counts and
the number with a recorded failure. A parent can still be pending while some
devices have succeeded; the device counts make partial failures visible. Failure
codes come from a fixed safe mapping. Unknown stored error text becomes
`delivery_failed_or_ambiguous`; it is never rendered or returned. Dead rows with
no recorded error use `retry_exhausted`. A provider acceptance status is not proof
of actual user receipt, nor an exactly-once delivery guarantee.

Optional query parameters are `limit` (1–100, default 25), `status` (pending,
leased, delivered, sent, cancelled, dead or failed), and `cursor`. Empty/absent status
shows all states. `failed` includes recorded parent errors, stopped parent jobs and
partial push-device failures even when the parent is still pending or accepted. Pagination orders by queue source then stable job ID, not by
newest timestamp. Cursors bind the account and status filter. Changing a filter
starts a new traversal. Reads are consistent within each response; later pages
reflect live queue changes rather than a retained historical snapshot. The page
has native filters, pagination and refresh links without JavaScript. Responses
use `Cache-Control: no-store, private`.

Pending may mean a scheduled time, quiet hours or transport retry; the page does
not infer a provider outage from a pending row. Leased means a worker owns the job
until the displayed expiry; an expired lease can be reclaimed by the existing
worker. This feature performs no mutation, purge, forced resend, retry-all or
provider request. Correct notification preferences, storage/SMTP/VAPID service
configuration or expired device subscriptions through their existing settings;
operational repair and retention policies remain explicit administrator work.

# Loading states

Server-rendered pages (Home, lists, spaces, search results, trash, sharing forms, account, delivery and authentication) arrive with confirmed data. Keep confirmed content visible during background refreshes and saves. A new destination immediately hides the old page and shows a spinner, before its HTML arrives.

Client-loaded content uses `beginLoading` from `assets/loading.js`. Spinners are the default whenever content size or shape is unknown: task trees, mixed lists, files, discussion, activity, search results and fetched dialogs. Skeletons are explicit choices for predictable forms, single-line values and calendar grids. Unknown controls stay hidden and inert. Placeholders contain no focusable controls and respect reduced motion.

Task side panels use a small spinner instead of predicting a task layout: descriptions, subtasks and attachments vary. The spinner appears after 150 ms to avoid flashing during fast loads, respects reduced motion, and leaves panel dimensions and the close control stable. The task HTML already contains the authorized subtree, planning, tags and rendered discussion/files. Controllers reuse these snapshots, so showing the panel needs no follow-up data reads. Mount controllers behind one spinner to avoid a second loading phase. Failures reveal the affected section’s retry state. The same loading owner handles cancellation, errors and retry.

Settings, welcome and notification templates include `data-loading-pending` so unconfirmed content cannot flash before their JavaScript module arrives. CSS provides an immediate spinner until the module takes ownership.

Call `finish()` in `finally`. For a failed initial load, `fail(message, retry)` removes the animation, keeps unknown values hidden and exposes a retry action. Preserve recoverable drafts instead of hiding them behind a failure. Each container has one current loading owner: a superseded response cannot dismiss the latest placeholder or insert a stale failure.

Use `preserve: true` on refresh after data has loaded. This sets `aria-busy` without removing, hiding or blocking the content. Inbox and Plan also skip unchanged renders and defer changed renders while a pointer interaction or input edit is in progress. Range changes conceal the old range until the new result arrives. Writes retain their existing draft, confirmation and save-feedback behaviour.

Coverage includes Inbox/Plan, notification center and bell, General/AI/Security settings, device status, onboarding, task previews/editor, quick capture, scheduling, metadata and search pickers, discussion/files, sharing/public access, activity, hierarchy, task breakdown and release information. Static screens require no synthetic loading phase.

`loading-states.spec.js` uses delayed and failed requests against an isolated development instance. It checks geometry, hidden defaults, retry, background refresh, dialog cancellation, notifications, search races, task panels, reduced motion and a mobile viewport. Existing settings and welcome tests exercise persistence and interaction after loading.

List headings reserve the color picker's full hit area. Capture and section controls,
task progress and summaries, discussion controls and the navigation logo render
with their final structure. Custom colors arrive in a render-blocking, immutable
palette stylesheet; navigation constructs validated palette rules synchronously
before swapping. Sidebar favorites, list entries and space cards share these
rules. `stable-render.spec.js` stalls scripts and compares initial/final geometry,
colors and controls. It also checks capture overflow at 320–1280px.

# Local SQLite recovery

`scripts/rebuild-backup.py` uses Python's standard-library SQLite online backup API. It supports current Rust rebuild databases only: it requires the rebuild tables and a contiguous migration history, and rejects legacy databases identified by `spaces` or `users.uuid`. It does not migrate a legacy database, contact a remote service, or implement Litestream/cloud replication.

Create the destination directory yourself, then choose a **new, nonexistent** filename:

```sh
python3 scripts/rebuild-backup.py backup /path/to/rebuild.sqlite3 /path/to/backups/rebuild-copy.sqlite3
python3 scripts/rebuild-backup.py restore /path/to/backups/rebuild-copy.sqlite3 /path/to/recovery/new-rebuild.sqlite3
```

Both commands perform the same verified database copy. The source is opened with a read-only SQLite URI; the destination is created exclusively with permissions 0600. Existing destinations (including symlinks), the source itself, and missing destination parent directories are refused. The script never overwrites a database. It verifies `PRAGMA integrity_check`, `PRAGMA foreign_key_check`, and rebuild schema identity before copying and again on the resulting file. Success prints only operation, verification status, and migration version numbers as JSON; failure prints a generic JSON error without filenames or database content and exits nonzero. A failed copy removes only its newly created destination file.

The SQLite backup API includes committed WAL content; copying the main `.sqlite3` file with a filesystem copy while the server is running does not provide that guarantee. The script does not checkpoint or write application rows in the source. SQLite may need existing readable WAL/shared-memory sidecars when opening a live database; it can manage shared-memory coordination even for read-only connections. Use a local filesystem supported by SQLite, keep the database and any live sidecars together, and do not pass `immutable=1` or remove WAL files while the source is running. The source and output contain private task data even though command output excludes it: keep their directory access restricted and manage retention explicitly.

Restore into an isolated directory first. Stop the server before changing its configured database path; point a separate local instance at the recovered copy and verify lists, task references, and recent edits before selecting it for ordinary use. Preserve the previous database and its sidecars for rollback. This tool intentionally does not replace the running database or change configuration for you. For future application versions, run recovery validation with a compatible rebuild version; the copy tool detects migration identity but does not interpret future schema semantics.

The synthetic integration test creates a fresh temporary database, leaves its writer open with committed WAL content, captures a task, backs up and restores to new paths, and verifies list count plus task ID/reference/description. It also verifies unchanged source main-file bytes and source task identity, refusal of existing/self/missing-parent destinations, and rejection of legacy/empty databases. All generated files are removed after the successful test. Run:

```sh
cargo test --manifest-path app/Cargo.toml --test backup
```

This is a verified local SQLite copy and isolated restore test, not a complete disaster-recovery system. It does not test power loss, remote retention, encryption at rest, filesystem failure, point-in-time recovery, or periodic restore drills. Once attachments or other external objects are introduced, backing up this database alone will not recover them: object bytes and database/object-key consistency will require a coordinated recovery process.

# Migration and export

## Source safety

The importer opens the legacy database read-only, runs SQLite's integrity check,
and uses SQLite's online backup API to build a consistent in-memory snapshot.
It does not migrate, delete, vacuum or write into the legacy database. Keep an
independent backup before applying an import. For a live SQLite database, use its
backup API or `.backup` command rather than copying only its main file while WAL
writers are active. The old application and its object bucket remain intact.

The actual legacy schema was inspected using schema queries only. Personal data
is not included in committed fixtures, examples, screenshots or command logs.
The optional real-copy validation test logs no records. All checked-in fixtures
are synthetic.

## Preview, then apply

```sh
cargo run -p todoer --bin todoer-migrate -- legacy \
  --source /private/legacy-copy.db --destination /private/rust.db

# Explicit application; use the same mapping for future reconciliations.
cargo run -p todoer --bin todoer-migrate -- legacy \
  --source /private/legacy-copy.db --destination /private/rust.db \
  --identity-map /private/identity-map.json --apply
```

Dry-run is the default. It validates the complete transaction in memory and
rolls it back. Existing destination data is copied read-only for a dry run; the
source and destination must be independent paths, not symlinks or hard links to
the same file. `--apply` alone authorizes writes to the separate Rust destination.
Reports contain counts, validation categories and credential-exclusion counts,
not task titles, descriptions, filenames or email addresses.

Identity maps have this form:

```json
{"users":{"OLD-USER-UUID":"EXISTING-RUST-USER-ID"}}
```

A flat old-ID-to-new-ID JSON object is also accepted. Targets must already exist
in the destination. Emails never match or merge identities automatically. Without
a mapping, users receive a `legacy:` identity with no authentication identity or
session, so they cannot sign in. To adopt real accounts, choose the explicit
mapping before first apply, or repeat into a fresh independent destination.
Changing a mapping on an existing imported source is a conflict, not an implicit
permission grant. Existing Rust edits are never overwritten by a reconciliation.

If the dry-run reports missing task sections, pass `--recovery-owner OLD-USER-UUID`
to preview recovery into a private workspace for that explicitly chosen legacy
user. The report counts missing sections and affected root tasks. Applying recovery
also requires that user to be explicitly mapped to an existing Rust account and
`--ack-unsupported` after reviewing every reported category. The original section
identifiers are retained; the original list and ownership cannot be inferred.
Use the same recovery owner and mapping on subsequent runs.

## Preserved data

Workspaces, lists, sections, task IDs, short references, sibling positions,
descriptions, completion state, nested subtasks, date-only due dates, priorities,
tags, comments and attachment references are materialized. Legacy archived tasks
become trash and retain their source archive flag in metadata. Archived spaces
keep their lists archived. Default flags, colors, sorting preferences, original
creation/update/completion timestamps, bookmarks, audit records, notification
read state, nonsecret settings and migration shadow tables are retained verbatim
in sanitized legacy metadata even where the new UI has no matching field.

Old migration shadow tables are archives. Only rows still referenced by live
tasks are materialized; unused historical rows remain in the metadata archive.
Every recognized sanitized source row is reconciled against an archived record.
Source and destination fingerprints detect source drift, changed mappings,
removed imported entities and concurrent edits. Re-running unchanged input is
safe. Updates that require reconciliation fail transactionally; no changed row
is silently replaced. Cycles, missing task parents, unsupported priorities/dates and invalid foreign-key
relationships fail validation. Recoverable missing hierarchy is handled explicitly
as described below, with acknowledgement required before apply.

Passwords, confirmation codes, TOTP material, AI API keys and unknown settings
values are excluded. Unknown tables are listed as unsupported and block apply
unless the operator explicitly passes `--ack-unsupported`; those tables are not
imported by that acknowledgement. Preserve the original backup for any future
conversion of unsupported structures. No source row is printed to diagnose it.

Legacy attachment keys are the original UUID object keys, not signed URLs.
Their filename, MIME, size and source timestamps remain in
`legacy_attachment_refs`. The importer does not claim an original checksum that
did not exist. A separately configured read-only legacy blob adapter verifies
size and computes a fresh baseline digest when a ZIP is created.

## Authorized exports

```sh
cargo run -p todoer --bin todoer-migrate -- export \
  --database /private/rust.db --actor EXISTING-USER-ID \
  --format json --output /private/export.json
```

Choose `--list ID` or `--workspace ID` to narrow the export; otherwise it covers
currently readable lists. The CLI is an administrative local tool. A future HTTP
adapter must derive actor identity from authentication, never a request-supplied
user ID. Exports use a consistent snapshot and current shared authorization
views before including data. ACLs appear only for owned workspaces. A directly
shared list does not disclose its original workspace title or other recipients.
Sessions, auth identities, Google claims, token hashes, invitation secrets,
provider secrets and delivery queues are never exported.

JSON format version 1 contains business tables plus lossless sanitized legacy
metadata. Plaintext is a readable task tree with IDs, completion status and
descriptions. CSV is a flat task export with explicit task/list/parent IDs,
position and revision; it does not encode sections, comments, attachments, tags,
ACLs or recurrence rules. Formula-like CSV cells are prefixed with an apostrophe;
newlines, quotes and delimiters use the maintained CSV encoder. Use JSON for a
full-fidelity metadata restore.

## JSON restore

```sh
cargo run -p todoer --bin todoer-migrate -- restore \
  --source /private/export.json --destination /private/restored.db \
  --identity-map /private/identity-map.json
# Add --apply only after reviewing the dry-run counts.
```

Only the versioned business-table allowlist is accepted. Mapping targets must
already exist. Unmapped users become disabled `import:` identities. Exported ACL
roles are preserved only through these explicit identities. Guest exports with
no disclosed owner ACL become private copied workspaces owned by the mapped
export recipient. Untracked existing entity IDs cause a conflict, preventing a
restore from granting access to an unrelated existing workspace. Repeating the
same bundle and mapping is safe; newer edits cause a conflict. Authentication
state and operational notification jobs are never imported.

## ZIP backup

Use `--format zip` with the normal private attachment configuration and, for old
blobs, separate `TODOER_LEGACY_STORAGE_*` configuration. ZIP files contain
`business.json`, attachment files named by safe UUIDs, and `manifest.json` with
MIME, byte length, SHA-256 and verification provenance. Legacy digests are labelled
as a first-capture baseline. New objects are checked against their stored digest.
Empty files are valid. Downloads are limited to 25 MiB per object and performed
one at a time; oversized, missing or unverifiable objects fail the entire export.
No partial archive is published. Business JSON is limited to 100 MiB.

Output files are created exclusively with mode 0600 on Unix. Existing files and
symlinks are never overwritten. Archive names do not use user filenames, so
`../` and path separators in filenames cannot escape the archive. Verification
checks every declared file without extracting it and rejects undeclared files.
The manifest excludes itself from its checksum list. JSON restore restores
metadata, not S3 bytes; ZIP restore verifies and restores those bytes using its
manifest as described below. No bucket object is mutated by export.

Legacy orphan hierarchy is recovered only for an existing source creator. Missing
lists receive a clearly named placeholder; lists with missing workspaces go into
a deterministic private recovery workspace owned by that creator. Original source
parent IDs remain in the sanitized archive. Dry-run reports recovery counts and
apply requires `--ack-unsupported`; deleted creator UUIDs are preserved as disabled local placeholder accounts, also requiring explicit acknowledgement. Non-UUID ownership references block import. Derived
reference indexes are excluded; original reference text is preserved.

## Complete ZIP restore

`todoer-migrate restore --source export.zip --destination restored.db` validates
without writing either storage or database. Add `--apply` only after reviewing
the report. ZIP is detected by its file signature. Apply uses the normal private
`TODOER_STORAGE_*` destination configuration, never the legacy source credentials.

The complete archive manifest, checksums, canonical attachment IDs, declared
sizes, metadata relationships and destination conflicts are checked before any
upload. Restores accept at most 10,000 manifest entries, 512 MiB of total declared
content, 100 MiB business JSON and 25 MiB per attachment. Empty objects work.
Every attachment must have exactly one matching archive entry; extra or missing
object files fail validation. Native metadata digests must match the manifest.

Objects use deterministic private restore keys derived from the bundle digest
and attachment UUID, not archive-supplied object keys or filenames. Uploads and
promotion use conditional creation and verify checksums, including existing
objects on retries. A different existing object is never overwritten. Original
attachment IDs remain stable. Legacy attachments become normal verified native
attachments; their original MIME, object key and metadata remain in sanitized
source records. Imported creation attribution for those legacy files is the
mapped export recipient.

The database commits only after all object staging and promotion checks succeed.
An interrupted restore can leave immutable objects with no committed metadata;
retrying the same archive safely reuses verified bytes. Database edits racing
with restore still cause the final metadata transaction to fail. There is no
cross-system rollback or deletion of preexisting objects. Retain source archives;
review unreachable restore objects separately before any retention cleanup.
JSON restore continues to restore metadata only; use ZIP for usable attachment
bytes. ZIP restore is covered by a local HTTP object-store roundtrip test that
retrieves the imported bytes, repeats conditional writes and rejects a corrupt
existing object without committing metadata or overwriting that object.

## HTTP transfers

Authenticated `GET /api/v1/export?format=json|text|csv|zip` exports the readable
account. Add either `list=ID` or `workspace=ID` to narrow it. Responses download
fixed filenames, use `Cache-Control: no-store, private` and `nosniff`, and stream
from exclusive mode-0600 temporary files which are removed after response or
cancellation. ZIP requires configured private storage, plus separate legacy blob
configuration when old attachment references are present.

`POST /api/v1/import` accepts a raw `application/zip` or `application/json` body.
It defaults to validation only. `?apply=true` explicitly applies. Browser session,
same-origin validation and `X-CSRF-Token` are required; bearer credentials cannot
import. Only the export recipient maps to the signed-in account. Other source
users stay separate disabled identities, and existing entity IDs or changed rows
are never implicitly overwritten. HTTP JSON with attachments is rejected: use
ZIP so attachment metadata cannot be restored without its bytes. Uploads stream
to private temporary files with a 512 MiB ZIP / 100 MiB JSON limit. No session,
provider token, password or delivery credential is included in exports.

# Notification center

The authenticated shell includes a bell with an unread badge, a five-item recent panel and a full `/notifications` page with All/Unread filters and 25-item cursor pagination. `/settings/notifications` controls categories, muted lists, quiet hours and email summaries; `/settings/devices` enables browser push. Public pages have no bell or private notification API access.

## Identity and delivery

- SQLite migration 036 stores inbox entries and read state per user. Shared task changes are recorded in the task mutation transaction and keyed by history sequence; authors do not notify themselves, including actions through their agent credentials. Existing history is not backfilled.
- Overdue open tasks are keyed by task and actual deadline, independently of priority/planned-date revisions. Date-only deadlines expire at the following local midnight in each recipient's timezone. A changed deadline creates a new alert if overdue. Existing overdue tasks are discovered on the first worker tick.
- Scheduled reminders are keyed by task, recipient and timestamp, merging email/push channel copies. Transport cancellation or disabled push does not remove the in-app reminder. Removing the reminder or completing the task hides it. A delivered reminder retained in a new schedule revision stays delivered and does not replay.
- Inbox rows reference live tasks instead of storing private title snapshots. Reads and badge counts recheck list access, task deletion/completion, list/space archival and current due/reminder schedules. Shared-change entries remain visible after task completion. Revoked access hides entries immediately.
- Shared updates and due alerts enqueue push only when opted in at creation. Explicit reminder pushes keep their existing delivery jobs, avoiding a second push from the inbox. Push reuses session-bound subscriptions, per-device leases, retry limits and live permission/preferences/read-state checks. Marking an entry read cancels unsent inbox push delivery. An already accepted push cannot be recalled.
- Push sends generic text and opens the notification center for due/shared alerts. Stable intent/device tags collapse retry duplicates in the browser; external delivery remains best effort, not exactly once. Email remains reminders/summaries, not a second email for every shared edit.

## Refresh and failure behavior

An independent server worker projects deadlines/reminders every 15 seconds even without SMTP or VAPID. The shell polls every 15 seconds while visible and online, refreshing immediately on reconnect/tab visibility. Failures back off to 30 seconds and preserve the last known badge. Bell and badge animate on a new entry, respecting reduced-motion preferences. Quiet hours defer external delivery, while in-app entries still appear.

Opening the panel does not mark anything read. Individual acknowledgements and “mark all as read” are server-confirmed; the latter includes only IDs through the last fetched watermark, preserving arrivals during an outstanding request. Read state synchronizes on other tabs/devices at their next poll. Notification data is never cached by the service worker.

# Planning and notification policy

Today includes incomplete planned or due tasks from the last year through today.
Upcoming covers the next fourteen days. Date-only planning and due values keep
their entered calendar date. Timed due values are projected into the account's
IANA timezone. Planning ranges are bounded to 366 days and return at most 10,000
scheduled tasks, with current list access checked before inclusion.

Weekly statistics count completion transitions of tasks marked as leaves at the
time of the event. Parent containers are excluded. Reopening then completing a
leaf counts another transition. Legacy history without a timestamp or leaf
snapshot is excluded; timestamps are never inferred from current task state.

Notification preferences are account settings. Email delivery defaults off.
Timezone, optional local quiet hours, daily and weekly opt-in, local delivery
clock times and per-list mute IDs are explicit. The browser preference endpoint
requires session authentication, origin checks and CSRF for writes. Scoped agent
credentials cannot inspect or change account-wide preference documents.

The scheduling REST interface uses common task revisions for schedule changes
and separate series revisions for pause/resume/stop. Recurring pages offer these
explicit controls; stopping preserves tasks and occurrence history. SMTP worker
delivery is documented below when configured; no push transport is advertised.

## SMTP worker

Configure `TODOER_SMTP_HOST` and `TODOER_SMTP_FROM` to enable a worker. Optional
`TODOER_SMTP_PORT` defaults to 587; `TODOER_SMTP_USERNAME` and
`TODOER_SMTP_PASSWORD` must be supplied together. STARTTLS is required by default;
set `TODOER_SMTP_TLS=implicit` for implicit TLS, normally port 465. Certificate
verification uses rustls and Mozilla trust roots. SMTP secrets are never stored in
SQLite or included in worker logs.

Production recipients come only from an identity registered with a verified
email, and must opt in. Arbitrary recipient addresses are not accepted from task
content. Per-list mutes, current task schedule revision, completion/trash state,
list archive state and current recipient permissions are checked immediately
before preparing each reminder. Preferences and quiet hours are read again for
send preparation. A permission change concurrent with an external send cannot
recall a message already accepted by SMTP.

Quiet hours defer an intent without consuming its retry allowance. Equal start
and end mute all hours. Overnight intervals work in the selected IANA timezone;
a nonexistent quiet-end time moves forward to the next valid minute. Explicit
email opt-out, missing verified recipient, muted lists, stale schedules and
unavailable email delivery cancel the affected email intent. Push reminders and daily/weekly push summaries are implemented separately; see [push](push.md) for session-bound devices, generic encrypted payloads and delivery limits.

The worker claims one reminder at a time, with a 60-second ownership lease.
Transport operations time out after at most 20 seconds. Failures retry with
bounded exponential backoff and a maximum of five claims, including crashes.
It checks shutdown between jobs. The server owns and awaits the returned worker
handle during graceful shutdown.

Daily and weekly digests are durable jobs with a unique `(user, kind, period)`.
They are created only for the current local delivery day after the selected clock
time. Missed days are not replayed as a backlog. Contents are recomputed at send
time from currently authorized, nonmuted tasks. Emails list at most 100 plaintext
titles and include the total scheduled open count; weekly digests also count leaf
completion transitions for that week. Daily summaries include the previous year
and tomorrow; weekly summaries use a bounded overdue window plus the next week.
Old periods, revoked opt-in and changed delivery weekdays are cancelled.

Each email uses the durable job ID as its stable `Message-ID`. SMTP cannot
promise exactly-once delivery: a network failure after server acceptance, or a
crash before SQLite acknowledgement, may cause a duplicate. `Message-ID` helps
receivers identify retries, but ordinary SMTP does not guarantee deduplication.
The database never marks a delivery successful before SMTP accepts it.

## Local capture check

Run `uv run --no-project --with aiosmtpd python scripts/rebuild-smtp-check.py`.
It starts an isolated local SMTP capture server and runs the ignored Rust worker
integration test. It verifies the envelope recipient, stable message ID format,
UTF-8 plaintext body and absence of replay after acknowledgement. Plain SMTP is
allowed only with `TODOER_SMTP_INSECURE_LOCAL=1` and a loopback host. The explicit
`TODOER_SMTP_TEST_RECIPIENT` adapter additionally requires an `.invalid` recipient;
it cannot redirect a production SMTP delivery.

Reminder intent identity is `(task, recipient, channel, resolved instant)`. Editing
priority/planned date or re-saving unchanged reminders reuses that delivery intent
and its push device ledger. A delivered instant is not sent again on such edits;
a different reminder instant creates a new intent. Exhausted attempts stay dead
until an explicit operational retry policy is used. In-flight SMTP acceptance
still has the documented crash/commit ambiguity; stable Message-ID is assistance,
not an exactly-once guarantee.

## Push digest channel

`push_daily_opt_in` and `push_weekly_opt_in` are independent, default-off fields
in the existing notification preferences document. They reuse the daily/weekly
clock, weekday, timezone, quiet hours and list mutes. The native preferences form
exposes both email and push choices. Push also requires account push opt-in and a
currently live device session; email opt-in and verified email are not gates for
push. Common queue/claim/timing functions serve separate SMTP and push outboxes,
so either worker can run without the other. Migration 021 adds push digest and
per-device delivery tables; existing email uniqueness and retry state stay intact.

Push summaries carry generic text and `/review`, never private task text/counts.
The send path rechecks current membership, mutes, opt-in and session. New timing
or quiet-hour rules defer outstanding work; stale local periods cancel. Durable
per-period and per-device identities prevent ordinary queue/retry duplication,
while provider acceptance before local commit retains the documented crash
ambiguity. See [push verification](push.md) for local HTTP evidence and real
device checks that remain external.

# Browser push reminders

The Rust rebuild implements encrypted Web Push for individual scheduled reminders, alongside the existing durable reminder outbox. `/settings/devices` enables a browser after an explicit click, lists registered devices, and supports revocation with a native form. Registration requires a production browser session, a CSRF token and configured VAPID delivery. Development-token and agent-token registration are refused. Browser or OS permission is separate from the account's push opt-in.

## Server configuration

- `TODOER_PUSH_VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`: persistent P-256 private scalar, 32 bytes encoded as URL-safe base64 without padding. Generate with a trusted Web Push/VAPID key tool and keep it secret; this is not a PEM document. The corresponding public key is derived server-side.
- `TODOER_PUSH_VAPID_SUBJECT`: operator contact, `mailto:…` or HTTPS URL, included in signed VAPID claims.
- `TODOER_PUSH_EXTRA_HOSTS`: optional comma-separated **exact** additional provider hostnames. This explicitly extends the egress allowlist; there are no URL, wildcard, IP-literal, non-443 or HTTP overrides.

Both VAPID variables absent disables delivery; partial or malformed configuration fails initialization. Keep the key stable across deployments: changing it requires browsers to unsubscribe and subscribe with the replacement public key. No push credentials come from object storage, legacy storage, SMTP or Litestream configuration. Endpoint URLs and encryption keys are necessary private subscription credentials stored in SQLite; API listings expose only their SHA256 endpoint fingerprint for browser matching, never the endpoint or encryption secrets. Ordinary backup access therefore also grants access to this sensitive metadata.

Allowed built-in HTTPS providers are `fcm.googleapis.com`, `updates.push.services.mozilla.com`, and subdomains of `push.apple.com`. Validation rejects userinfo, fragments, IP literals and custom ports. Delivery resolves DNS with a timeout, rejects private/local/reserved addresses, pins the checked answers, disables environment proxies and refuses redirects. Test-only loopback delivery is compiled exclusively under `cfg(test)` and is not an environment option.

## Sessions, policy and delivery

Each registration references the exact `auth_sessions.id` that registered it. Expiry, logout or session revocation makes that device ineligible immediately for future sends; signing in again requires explicit re-enablement. Revoking a device disables it server-side even if browser unsubscription fails. Account-wide opt-out disables delivery on every device. Existing notification quiet hours and list mute preferences apply, independently of email opt-in. The existing `Store::reminder_eligible` performs the live reminder lease, schedule, task state and current list permission check; push uses that common eligibility operation rather than a second scheduling rule engine. Delivery rechecks it and the session immediately before the HTTP request.

The shared reminder outbox is claimed by channel: the email worker never consumes push jobs. `push_deliveries` has a unique `(reminder_id,device_id)` row, a bounded-attempt lease, retry availability and terminal sent/dead state. Successful devices are not replayed when another device fails. Subscription revisions fence late responses from an older registration, so an expired response cannot disable a newly re-enabled device. `404`/`410` disables the expired subscription. `429` and server failures retry with bounded `Retry-After` (1–3600 seconds, numeric or HTTP date); other provider rejections become terminal. Network errors use redacted diagnostics. Five attempts per device bound retries, including abandoned leases. Ten devices per account and bounded per-job claim windows keep work within the common 60-second parent lease; unfinished devices resume in another tick. SQLite work runs on a blocking worker, and no database mutex remains held across HTTP I/O.

Payloads use RFC8188 `aes128gcm` encryption and signed VAPID authentication through pinned `web-push 0.11.0`, with existing `reqwest` transport. The payload has exactly these fields:

```json
{"title":"Todoer reminder","url":"/tasks/<task UUID>","intent_id":"<reminder UUID>:<device UUID>"}
```

There is no task title, description, comment, workspace name or list name. The canonical task URL checks current authorization again when opened. Deterministic per-device intent IDs and provider topics allow notification replacement. `TTL: 0` deliberately prevents a provider retaining an offline reminder that could become stale after logout; offline devices can miss reminders. This is a privacy/delivery tradeoff, not guaranteed delivery. An in-flight push accepted before logout and an already displayed notification cannot be recalled. As with email, a crash after provider acceptance but before the SQLite success commit can cause duplicate transport delivery; the stable notification tag reduces duplicate display, and does not establish exactly-once delivery.

Daily and weekly push digests use independent `push_daily_opt_in` and
`push_weekly_opt_in` notification preferences, both false by default. The native
notification settings form exposes each channel separately. Push uses the same
IANA timezone, daily/weekly clock, weekly weekday, quiet hours and per-list mutes
as email. Device/account push opt-in and a live registering session are also
required. Email opt-in never implicitly enables push summaries.

The common digest scheduler and timing policy supply separate
`push_digest_outbox` rows, unique by user/kind/local period. SMTP never claims
these jobs. The existing per-device delivery leases, bounded retries, dead
subscription handling and revision fences operate on `push_digest_deliveries`.
A successful device is not replayed when another device retries. A tick handles
at most one push reminder and one digest, with ten-second device-claim windows
per job plus bounded in-flight network requests. A remaining device resumes on a
later tick. Fresh opt-outs, timing changes, list permissions and sessions are
checked before transport; muted/all-inaccessible accounts receive no digest.
Missed old daily periods are cancelled rather than delivered as catch-up spam.

Digest payloads have the same three-field shape as reminders, with generic title
`Todoer summary` and URL `/review`. They contain no task details or counts. The
review page rechecks current authorization. Device permission,
foreground/background behavior and OS settings remain browser-controlled.

## Browser behavior

The settings controller feature-detects secure contexts, service workers, PushManager and Notifications. It prepares the public key and service worker before exposing the enable button, so `subscribe({userVisibleOnly:true,…})` stays in the direct user gesture. Denied permissions and unavailable server/browser support have explicit explanations. Enabling stores the subscription against the current login session; the browser cannot send arbitrary notification payloads. The disable operation revokes the matching account device first, then unsubscribes in the browser. Native device revocation remains available without JavaScript.

On iOS/iPadOS 16.4 and later, Web Push requires a Home Screen web app; normal browser tabs do not provide the same enablement flow. Safari/macOS and Chromium/Firefox behavior is feature-detected rather than inferred from a browser name. The service worker must display a user-visible notification and handle the canonical same-origin task link. Provider acceptance is not proof the OS displayed it.

### Registration failures and local display test

Browser permission does not guarantee that the browser has a working push
service. In particular, Helium has an [upstream push support

The old controller silently ignored that browser error as though the page had
been unmounted; it never reached the registration POST. Lifecycle cancellation

Enablement shows connection and save progress. A browser subscription still
pending after 30 seconds produces recovery guidance and releases the button.
Browser subscription operations cannot be cancelled: retry reuses the pending
promise, and a late result is saved only by an actively waiting attempt. Reload
starts a fresh controller. No timeout automatically unsubscribes a device.

**Test notification** uses the active service worker's `showNotification()` when
permission is granted. It checks local browser/OS display, including on browsers
whose remote push service is unavailable. The result explicitly explains that
it does not test server/provider delivery. Browser and OS settings can suppress
notifications even when this API resolves.

The isolated `app/browser/push-registration.spec.js` fixture serves synthetic

It covers visible/retryable browser AbortError, a pending subscription timeout
and late completion without duplicate POSTs, and the local display test. Run

# Tags, sections, task ordering and references

Tags have opaque UUIDs, display names and revisions. Their home is the task's workspace, or its list for legacy lists without a workspace. Names are trimmed and compared with Rust Unicode lowercase; this is not Unicode NFC normalization or locale-specific case folding. A name contains 1–100 non-control characters. A task accepts at most 50 tags, supplied as names or explicit `{ "id": "TAG_UUID" }` selectors. Duplicate normalized names share one tag in a home. Task tag changes require the current task revision. Renaming a workspace tag requires workspace editing permission; a guest's access to one shared list does not grant that authority.

A guest sees only tags attached to tasks they can currently read. They cannot enumerate the parent workspace's other tags. Cross-workspace moves remap tags by normalized name into the destination home and record old/new tag IDs in `tag_move_audit`. The move preserves display names without exposing the source home. Existing destination names are reused. The move hook runs inside the same transaction and clears section assignment.

Section assignment applies to a root and its whole active subtree. Descendants inherit the root section, including children created later. Assigning a child independently is rejected. A section must belong to the task's list. Same-list reparenting rejects cycles, inherits the new parent's section and reopens a completed new ancestor when necessary. Cross-list moves use the existing subtree move operation and its access-change acknowledgement.

Sibling ordering takes a list revision and the exact set of active sibling IDs. Missing, extra or repeated IDs fail; stale list revisions conflict. The transaction bumps the list revision, updates sibling positions and revisions, and writes task history. Reparenting and section assignment likewise require the current task revision.

Reference prefixes are:

| Prefix | Target | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@` | Space | `@[Weekly planning]` |
| `#` | List | `#Groceries` or `#LIST_UUID` |
| `$` | Section | `$[Next steps]` |
| `%` | Top-level task | `%T-existing-reference`, `%TASK_UUID`, or an unambiguous UUID prefix of at least eight characters |
| `^` | Subtask at any depth | `^TASK_ID` or `^[Task title]` |
| `+` | Tag | `+urgent` or `+[high priority]` |

Task and subtask prefixes follow the current parent relationship, including after reparenting. `%` resolves only top-level tasks; `^` resolves only tasks with a parent. Autocomplete choices include their canonical `prefix`. Existing saved reference bindings keep their target IDs and rendered links.

Bare names use letters, digits, underscores and hyphens; brackets allow spaces and other literal name characters. Trailing punctuation remains ordinary text. Code spans, fenced code blocks, existing Markdown links/images, escaped prefixes, email addresses and prefixes embedded in words do not become references. Parsing uses CommonMark events and source ranges. Rendering injects typed link/text events and sanitizes the resulting HTML with the same image-removal policy as ordinary Markdown.

Resolution checks live authorization before returning any candidate. Exact opaque IDs and full task references identify their targets directly. Duplicate names remain plain text and return accessible choices; the system does not pick a target by ordering. Autocomplete returns at most 30 choices and examines at most 1000 candidates per entity kind. Name resolution shares that bounded candidate window; an explicit full ID can resolve targets outside it. Each description or comment indexes at most 200 reference occurrences. Use full IDs for reliable disambiguation in large collections.

`reference_edges` stores source kind/ID, occurrence index, target kind/ID and the original token. `reference_sources` stores the exact content hash. The application indexes saved task descriptions and comment bodies inside their write transaction. An unchanged hash preserves every existing binding: renaming or moving an entity never silently redirects a link to a different entity with the old name. Unbound occurrences can return fresh accessible choices for explicit review without being automatically bound.

Rendering requires the saved source text and a matching hash, then checks each target's current visibility. It displays the current target label and URL. Deleted, inaccessible or unavailable targets fall back to the original token as plain text; their current title is not revealed. Unindexed text uses ordinary sanitized Markdown. Backlinks return source kind/ID plus the authorized `source_task_id`, require access to the target and each current, non-deleted source, and ignore stale source hashes. Listing backlinks is capped at 100 visible sources.

The domain tests exercise Unicode names and collisions, revision conflicts, shared-list privacy, scope remapping and audit records, section inheritance, cycle rejection, sibling ordering, CommonMark exclusions, bracketed names, duplicate ambiguity, stable links after renames, hidden/deleted targets, safe HTML labels and authorized backlinks. Run `cargo test --locked taxonomy::tests --lib`.

REST exposes the same operations through `/api/v1/lists/{id}/tags`, `/api/v1/tags/{id}`, task `/tags`, `/section`, `/reparent`, and list `/task-order` endpoints. Compact typed actions are available at `POST /api/v1/organize`. Workspace members can list the tag registry; direct list guests see only tags currently used in that list. Standalone workspace-tag creation requires workspace editing permission; a direct guest can create and assign a name in an authorized task update without enumerating unused tags.

Reference resolve/autocomplete, source unresolved occurrences, explicit binding, and target backlinks are exposed under `/api/v1/references`, with a compact action endpoint at `POST /api/v1/references`. Resolve always returns a structured `choices` array, including zero/multiple choices. Explicit binding supplies the current saved source revision, occurrence index, and chosen target kind/ID. The target must remain an accessible exact candidate. A successful bind increments the task or comment revision, keeps the saved text unchanged, and preserves other bindings; stale requests conflict. Task source IDs can be opaque IDs or full task references. The CLI and MCP schemas document the same actions; no adapter implements separate mutation rules.

## Recovery into a new path

Stop application writes for an eventual cutover; first rehearse in isolation.
Keep the damaged/current DB and its WAL/SHM files intact in a separate safe location.
Use the same replica configuration and credentials to restore into a **new** path:

```sh
litestream restore -config deploy/litestream.yml \
  -o /isolated/restore/todoer.db -integrity-check full "$TODOER_RUST_DB"
```

Add `-timestamp RFC3339` for an available historical recovery boundary. Do not use

adapters; avoid replaying real reminders during a rehearsal. An authenticated
Google rehearsal needs a separately configured callback origin.

immutable, private, and retained after soft deletion; application GC is disabled.

referenced by every supported DB recovery point, including archived legacy UUID
objects. Do not add an object lifecycle rule that deletes them after the DB window

older binary against a schema it does not support. Rehearse a restore rather than
